overview: Git tracks changes to files in three distinct areas: the working directory (the files you edit on disk), the staging area (also called the index, where you queue exactly what will go into the next snapshot), and the repository (the permanent history of committed snapshots).

The everyday cycle is: edit files in the working directory, choose which changes to stage with git add, review the difference between what is staged and what is not with git diff, and then capture a snapshot with git commit that becomes a permanent, referenceable point in history.

History tools let you read that record: git log lists commits, git show inspects one, git blame reveals who last changed each line, and .gitignore keeps data files and secrets out of the repo - while git revert and git reset let you safely (or dangerously) undo mistakes.
learningObjectives: Explain the three areas - working directory, staging area (index), and repository - and use git status and git diff to see exactly what is modified, staged, and committed.
Stage changes selectively with git add (including git add -p for partial staging), craft focused atomic commits with git commit, and fix the last commit with git commit --amend.
Read and search history with git log/show/blame, reference commits with SHA and HEAD~n, ignore files with .gitignore, and undo changes safely with git revert versus destructively with git reset.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Git is a distributed version-control system that records the state of a project as a series of immutable snapshots called commits. Each commit stores a full tree of file contents, references its parent commit(s), and is identified by a 40-character SHA-1 hash. Git models three areas: the working directory (the checked-out files you edit), the staging area or index (a list of changes proposed for the next commit), and the local repository (the object database of commits, trees, and blobs in the .git directory). git add copies changes from the working directory into the index; git commit writes the index into a new commit object and advances the current branch pointer (HEAD). The commit graph is a directed acyclic graph in which HEAD points to the current commit, HEAD~1 its parent, and so on. Undoing is achieved either by git revert (which creates a new commit that inverts a prior one, preserving history) or git reset (which moves the branch pointer and, depending on mode, the index and working directory, rewriting history).
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of Git like packing photos into an album. Your working directory is your desk, covered with photos you are still editing and rearranging. The staging area is the small tray where you place only the photos you have decided belong on the next album page - you choose exactly which ones, and you can put some back on the desk if you change your mind. When the tray looks right, git commit glues that page permanently into the album (the repository) with a note describing it. git status is you glancing at the desk and tray to see what has changed and what is queued. git diff shows the pen marks - what is different on the desk versus what is in the tray. git log is flipping back through the finished album pages, and git blame is checking the caption on each photo to see who added it and when. A .gitignore is a rule saying 'never put my private diary or these giant raw files in the album'. And when a page turns out wrong, git revert adds a new page that corrects it (leaving the record honest), while git reset can rip pages out - powerful, but you can lose work.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Git was created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds to manage Linux kernel development after the kernel team lost free access to the proprietary BitKeeper tool. He wanted something fast, fully distributed, and able to guarantee integrity, so Git stores content addressed by cryptographic hash and gives every developer a complete copy of history. This was a break from earlier centralized systems like CVS and Subversion, where history lived on one server and most operations required a network round-trip. The staging area (the index) was one of Git's distinctive design choices: rather than commit everything you have changed, you assemble a commit deliberately, which encourages small, focused, reviewable changes. Git's speed and offline capability made branching and merging cheap, which in turn enabled modern collaborative workflows. The rise of hosting platforms such as GitHub (2008) and GitLab made Git the near-universal standard, and today it underpins how data engineers version SQL, dbt models, Airflow DAGs, and pipeline code with the same rigor software engineers apply to application code.

whyItMatters.business: Version control is the audit trail for the code that runs the business's data: when a dashboard number looks wrong, git log and git blame let a team trace exactly which change, by whom, and when introduced the problem, turning a frightening incident into a quick, evidence-based fix and rollback.
whyItMatters.engineering: Committing an ETL, SQL, or dbt change as a small, self-contained atomic unit makes code reviewable, revertible, and understandable; the staging area lets engineers separate unrelated edits into clean commits instead of one giant, unreviewable blob.
whyItMatters.scalability: As teams and pipelines grow, a shared, hashed history lets many engineers work in parallel, review each other's changes, and reconstruct the exact state of the code that produced any past run, without stepping on one another.
whyItMatters.cost: Being able to revert a bad transformation commit in seconds - rather than manually reconstructing what a query used to look like - avoids prolonged incidents, wasted recompute, and the labor cost of forensic guesswork about what changed.
whyItMatters.reliability: A disciplined commit history plus a .gitignore that keeps credentials and large data files out of the repo makes deployments reproducible and safe: you can pin production to a known-good commit and roll back with git revert without ever hand-editing files under pressure.

coreComponents.name: Working directory (modified files)
coreComponents.definition: The set of actual files checked out on disk that you open and edit; Git compares them against the last commit and the staging area to classify each file as untracked, modified, or unchanged.
coreComponents.purpose: To give you a normal folder of files to work in while Git watches what you change relative to the recorded history.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Hold your live edits, surface as 'untracked' (new, never added) or 'modified' (tracked but changed) in git status, and be the source Git copies from when you run git add. Changes here are not yet recorded and can be discarded with git restore.
coreComponents.examples: edit pipeline.sql | create new_model.sql (untracked) | git status shows 'Changes not staged for commit' | git restore pipeline.sql to discard edits

coreComponents.name: Staging area / index (what is queued for the next commit)
coreComponents.definition: An intermediate list, stored in .git/index, of exactly the changes you have marked to include in your next commit; git add moves changes here and git restore --staged removes them.
coreComponents.purpose: To let you deliberately assemble a focused, atomic commit from a subset of your working-directory changes instead of committing everything at once.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Record the proposed contents of the next snapshot, appear as 'Changes to be committed' in git status, be shown by git diff --staged, and be selectively populated with git add file, git add ., or git add -p for hunk-by-hunk staging.
coreComponents.examples: git add pipeline.sql | git add -p (stage some hunks) | git diff --staged | git restore --staged pipeline.sql (unstage)

coreComponents.name: Repository (committed history)
coreComponents.definition: The object database inside the .git directory that stores every commit as an immutable snapshot with a parent, an author, a message, and a unique SHA hash; the current branch pointer (via HEAD) marks where you are.
coreComponents.purpose: To provide a permanent, tamper-evident record of the project's states so any past version can be inspected, reproduced, or restored.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Store commits and their content, link each to its parent to form the history graph, advance the branch pointer when you commit, and let HEAD, HEAD~1, and SHAs address specific points for git log/show/checkout/revert/reset.
coreComponents.examples: git commit -m "Fix revenue join" | git log --oneline | git show HEAD | git show a1b2c3d | HEAD~3 references three commits back

coreComponents.name: History and undo tools (log, show, blame, revert, reset, .gitignore)
coreComponents.definition: The commands that read the committed history (log, show, blame, diff), decide what Git ignores (.gitignore), and undo changes either safely (revert) or destructively (reset).
coreComponents.purpose: To investigate when and why the code reached its current state and to correct mistakes cleanly without hand-editing files.
coreComponents.responsibilities: List/filter history (git log with --oneline/--graph/--author/--since/-- path), inspect a commit (git show), attribute lines (git blame), keep files out of the repo (.gitignore), and undo via git revert (new inverse commit) or git reset --soft/--mixed/--hard.
coreComponents.examples: git log --oneline --graph | git blame pipeline.sql | git revert a1b2c3d | git reset --soft HEAD~1 | echo '*.csv' >> .gitignore

internalWorking: Git stores content, not diffs: when you commit, Git compresses each file's contents into a 'blob' object named by the SHA-1 hash of its contents, records the folder structure as 'tree' objects, and wraps them in a 'commit' object that also stores the author, message, timestamp, and the SHA of the parent commit - so a commit is a full snapshot addressed by a hash, and identical content is stored only once.

The staging area is a real file (.git/index) that lists the paths and blob hashes proposed for the next commit. git add reads a file from the working directory, writes its current contents as a blob, and records that blob's hash in the index; this is why staging captures a file as it was at the moment you ran git add, and later edits are 'not staged' until you add again.

git status works by making three comparisons: index versus HEAD (the last commit) tells it what is 'staged / to be committed', and working directory versus index tells it what is 'modified but not staged'; files present on disk but absent from both are reported as 'untracked'. git diff shows working-directory-versus-index changes, while git diff --staged shows index-versus-HEAD changes.

git commit takes the current index, writes any new tree objects, creates a new commit object pointing at that tree and at the current commit as its parent, and then advances the current branch pointer (which HEAD follows) to the new commit. Because each commit records its parent, the commits form a directed acyclic graph that git log walks backward from HEAD, and references like HEAD~1 simply follow parent links.

Undo commands differ in what they touch. git revert reads an old commit, computes the inverse of its changes, and records that inverse as a brand-new commit on top of history - nothing is rewritten. git reset instead moves the current branch pointer to an earlier commit; --soft leaves the index and working directory alone (changes become staged again), --mixed (the default) also resets the index (changes become unstaged), and --hard additionally overwrites the working directory to match, permanently discarding those changes.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Edit files (working directory) -> git status / git diff to see what changed -> git add selects changes into the staging area (index) -> git diff --staged to review the queued snapshot -> git commit writes the index into a new commit and advances HEAD (repository) -> git log / git show / git blame read history -> undo via git revert (new inverse commit) or git reset (move HEAD, optionally discard)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. You edit a dbt model file, models/revenue.sql, to fix a wrong join. On disk the file is now changed; git status reports it under 'Changes not staged for commit' as modified, and git diff shows the exact lines you altered (red for removed, green for added).

2. You decide only the join fix belongs in this commit, not some unrelated formatting you also tried, so you run 'git add -p models/revenue.sql' and stage just the join hunk. git status now lists that hunk under 'Changes to be committed', while the rest stays unstaged.

3. You verify the queued snapshot with 'git diff --staged', which shows exactly what the commit will contain - only the join fix. This is the discipline the staging area exists for: crafting a focused, atomic, reviewable change.

4. You capture it with 'git commit -m "Fix revenue join to use customer_id"'. Git writes the index into a new commit object with a parent link and a fresh SHA (say a1b2c3d), and advances the branch pointer; 'git log --oneline' now shows your commit at the top.

5. Weeks later a report looks wrong. You run 'git log --oneline -- models/revenue.sql' to find changes to that file, 'git blame models/revenue.sql' to see which commit last touched the suspect line, and 'git show a1b2c3d' to read the change. Confirming a1b2c3d is the culprit and it is already pushed, you undo it safely with 'git revert a1b2c3d', which adds a new commit that reverses the bad join - preserving an honest history and letting you redeploy immediately.

keyTerminology.meaning: An immutable snapshot of the whole project at a point in time, storing its content, author, message, and parent, identified by a unique 40-character SHA hash (often abbreviated to 7 characters like a1b2c3d).
keyTerminology.importance: The commit is the atomic unit of history: every review, rollback, and investigation refers to a commit by its SHA, HEAD, or HEAD~n, so understanding it is the basis for everything else in Git.

keyTerminology.meaning: The intermediate list of changes you have marked (with git add) to include in the next commit, distinct from both your unsaved working-directory edits and the committed history.
keyTerminology.importance: It is what lets you build a focused, atomic commit from a subset of your changes; not understanding it is the source of most beginner confusion about 'why didn't my change get committed?'

keyTerminology.meaning: HEAD is a pointer to the commit you currently have checked out (the tip of your branch); HEAD~1 is its parent, HEAD~3 is three commits back, giving relative addresses into history.
keyTerminology.importance: These references let you talk about commits without copying long SHAs - essential for commands like git reset HEAD~1, git show HEAD~2, and comparing recent versions.

keyTerminology.meaning: A file listing path patterns Git should not track, such as *.csv, __pycache__/, and .env, so those files never appear as untracked or get committed.
keyTerminology.importance: It keeps credentials, large data files, and generated artifacts out of the repository - critical in data engineering, where accidentally committing a secret or a multi-gigabyte CSV is a serious mistake.

keyTerminology.meaning: git revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous one while keeping all history intact; git reset moves the branch pointer to an earlier commit and can discard commits and (with --hard) working-directory changes.
keyTerminology.importance: Choosing correctly is the difference between a safe, shareable undo (revert, right for pushed/shared history) and a destructive rewrite (reset, only safe on local, unshared commits).

importantConcepts.concept: Why the staging area exists: crafting atomic commits
importantConcepts.explanation: Many version-control systems commit everything you have changed in one go. Git adds a deliberate middle step - the staging area - so you decide precisely what goes into each commit. This matters because good history is made of small, self-contained, atomic commits: one commit that fixes a join, another that renames a column, rather than a single messy commit mixing both. With 'git add -p' you can even split one file's edits into separate commits by staging some hunks and not others. The payoff is huge in data engineering: reviewers can understand a focused change, git log tells a coherent story, git blame points to a meaningful commit, and git revert can undo exactly one logical change without collateral damage. The staging area is the tool that turns a chaotic set of edits into a clean, reviewable, revertible narrative.

importantConcepts.concept: git add stages a snapshot, it does not save your work
importantConcepts.explanation: A common beginner belief is that 'git add' saves progress. It does not. git add copies the file's current contents into the staging area as a proposal for the next commit; only 'git commit' records anything into history. Two consequences follow. First, if you edit a file after staging it, those new edits are not staged - git status will show the file as both 'staged' (the earlier version) and 'not staged' (the newer edits), and you must git add again to include them. Second, staged-but-uncommitted work is not protected: it lives only in the index and working directory, not in a commit, so it is easy to lose. The mental model to keep is: working directory (edits) -> staging area (git add: queued for next snapshot) -> repository (git commit: permanently recorded). Nothing is truly durable until it is committed - and even then, 'committed' means local, not backed up remotely (that is what push does).

These answer two different questions, and mixing them up causes confusion. 'git diff' with no arguments compares your working directory to the staging area - it shows changes you have made but not yet staged ('what would git add pick up?'). 'git diff --staged' (also written --cached) compares the staging area to the last commit (HEAD) - it shows exactly what your next commit will contain ('what did git add already queue?'). So after you 'git add' a file, it disappears from plain 'git diff' and appears in 'git diff --staged'. The disciplined workflow is: run 'git diff' to review edits before staging, then 'git diff --staged' immediately before committing to confirm the commit's contents are exactly what you intend - no debug prints, no stray credentials, no unrelated changes.

importantConcepts.concept: revert versus reset --soft/--mixed/--hard: safe versus destructive undo
importantConcepts.explanation: Undoing in Git has two philosophies. git revert is additive and safe: it creates a brand-new commit that applies the inverse of a target commit, so the bad change is neutralized while the full history - including the mistake and its reversal - remains visible. This is the correct tool for undoing a commit that has already been pushed or shared, because it does not rewrite anyone's history. git reset is subtractive and rewrites history by moving the branch pointer backward, and its three modes differ in how much they touch: '--soft HEAD~1' undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged (useful to recommit with a better message or split); '--mixed HEAD~1' (the default) also unstages them, leaving the edits in your working directory; '--hard HEAD~1' additionally discards the working-directory changes entirely - permanent data loss with no undo. The rule of thumb: use revert for anything already pushed; use reset only on local, unpushed commits, and treat '--hard' with extreme caution because it deletes uncommitted work.

variationsAndTypes: **Staging commands:** git add file (stage one file), git add . (stage everything under the current directory), git add -p (interactively stage hunk by hunk), git add -A (stage all changes including deletions).
**Inspecting state:** git status (untracked/modified/staged summary), git diff (working vs index), git diff --staged (index vs last commit), git diff HEAD (all uncommitted changes vs last commit).

**Committing:** git commit -m "subject" (message inline), git commit (opens editor for subject + body), git commit -a (stage all tracked modifications then commit), git commit --amend (replace the last commit to fix its message or add forgotten changes).

**Reading history:** git log --oneline (compact), --graph (branch topology), --stat (files changed), -p (full diffs), --author / --since / --grep (filter), and 'git log -- path' plus git show <sha> and git blame <file>.

**Undoing:** git restore file (discard working-dir edits), git restore --staged file (unstage), git revert <sha> (safe inverse commit), git reset --soft/--mixed/--hard <ref> (rewrite history, increasing destructiveness).
advantages: **Focused, reviewable commits:** the staging area lets you assemble small atomic commits, so each change to an ETL or SQL model is easy to review, understand, and revert independently.
**Complete, tamper-evident history:** every state is a hashed snapshot, so you can reproduce or inspect the exact code that produced any past pipeline run.
**Fast, safe rollback:** git revert undoes a bad commit in seconds by adding an inverse commit, without hand-editing files or losing history.
**Precise attribution and forensics:** git log, git show, and git blame let you trace when and why a pipeline bug was introduced and by whom.
**Keeps junk and secrets out:** .gitignore prevents credentials, large data files, and generated artifacts from ever entering the repository.
disadvantages: **Steep mental model:** the three areas (working, staged, committed) and the many undo variants confuse beginners, leading to lost work or malformed commits.
**Destructive commands have no undo:** git reset --hard and force-pushing rewritten history can permanently delete work if used carelessly.
**Poor for large binary/data files:** Git stores full snapshots, so committing big CSVs or Parquet files bloats the repo and slows everything - it is not a data store.
**Discipline is required:** without conventions, history degrades into huge 'misc changes' commits with useless messages, negating most of Git's value.
**Secrets are sticky:** a credential committed once stays in history even after deletion, requiring painful history rewrites to fully remove.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use staging and small commits whenever you change code, config, SQL, dbt models, or DAGs so each logical change is atomic and reviewable. Use git revert to undo commits that have already been pushed or shared. Use git reset (soft/mixed) locally to reshape unpushed commits, and .gitignore for every file that is a secret, large, or generated.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid committing large data files, datasets, or binaries to Git - use object storage or Git LFS instead. Avoid git reset --hard and history rewrites on shared branches, where they can destroy others' work. Avoid one giant commit mixing unrelated changes, and avoid ever committing secrets even 'temporarily', since removing them from history is costly.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Working with Git is like preparing a legal case file that becomes a permanent public record. Your desk is the working directory: documents you are still marking up and rearranging. Before anything goes on the record, you place selected pages into a submission folder - the staging area - choosing exactly which pages belong to this filing and leaving the rest on your desk (git add, and git restore --staged to pull one back out). When the folder is right, you file it with the court clerk, who stamps it with a unique case number and the date and binds it permanently into the record (git commit with its SHA). Later, anyone can read back through the filed record (git log), pull one filing to examine it (git show), or check the margin notes to see who submitted each line (git blame). A confidentiality rule keeps private documents out of the public record entirely (.gitignore). And if a filing turns out to be wrong, the honest fix is to file a correction that supersedes it (git revert) rather than secretly shredding pages from the bound record (git reset --hard), which destroys the trail.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Running git add saves my work.
commonMisconceptions.reality: git add only copies the file's current contents into the staging area as a proposal for the next commit; nothing is recorded in history until you run git commit. If you edit the file again after adding, those new edits are not staged. Only a commit turns your changes into a durable, referenceable point in history.

commonMisconceptions.myth: git reset --hard and git revert do the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They are opposites in safety. git revert adds a new commit that undoes a previous one while keeping all history intact - safe for shared/pushed commits. git reset --hard moves the branch pointer backward and permanently discards commits and uncommitted working-directory changes, rewriting history - dangerous, and never safe on shared branches.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Once I commit, my work is backed up.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A commit only records your change in your local repository, on your machine. It is not on the server or anyone else's machine until you run git push. If your laptop dies before pushing, committed-but-unpushed work is gone. Commit records history locally; push shares and backs it up remotely.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Keep repositories lean by excluding large data files with .gitignore (or Git LFS for genuinely needed binaries), and split unrelated pipelines into focused commits so history stays readable as the team and codebase grow; huge 'kitchen-sink' commits do not scale to code review.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Treat pushed commits as immutable: undo them with git revert rather than reset so deploys are reproducible and you can always pin production to a known-good SHA and roll back cleanly under pressure without hand-editing files.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Because a commit is only local until pushed, push frequently so a lost machine does not lose history; protect key branches so a stray reset --hard or force-push cannot destroy shared work.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Use git log with --since, --author, and '-- path' to audit what changed in a pipeline over a time window, and git blame to attribute a suspect line to the commit and person that introduced it when investigating an incident.
productionConsiderations.security: Never commit secrets: put .env, credentials, and key files in .gitignore, scan commits for secrets in CI, and if a secret does land in history, rotate it immediately and rewrite history to purge it - deletion in a later commit is not enough because it remains in old commits.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Fast, correct rollbacks with git revert shorten incidents and avoid wasted recompute and forensic labor; keeping data files out of Git avoids ballooning clone times and storage costs across every engineer's machine and CI runner.
productionConsiderations.performance: A small, well-pruned repository (no large binaries, sensible .gitignore) clones and checks out fast in CI/CD; use --oneline and path filters on git log to keep history browsing responsive on long-lived repos.

codeExamples.title: The stage -> diff -> commit cycle: working directory versus staging area
codeExamples.overview: Edit a pipeline file, inspect what changed, selectively stage it, review the queued snapshot, and commit it as one atomic change.
codeExamples.code:
# 1) See the current state: what is untracked, modified, or staged
git status

# 2) You edited pipeline.sql. See the UNSTAGED changes
#    (working directory vs staging area)
git diff pipeline.sql

# 3) Stage just this file into the index (the staging area)
git add pipeline.sql

# 4) Status now shows it under 'Changes to be committed'
git status

# 5) Plain 'git diff' is now empty for this file; review what is
#    STAGED instead (staging area vs last commit)
git diff --staged

# 6) Commit the staged snapshot with a clear, imperative message
git commit -m "Fix customer join in pipeline.sql to use customer_id"

# 7) Confirm the new commit is at the top of history
git log --oneline -1
codeExamples.breakdown: 'git status' summarizes untracked, modified (not staged), and staged files. 'git diff pipeline.sql' shows working-directory-vs-index changes - what git add would pick up. 'git add pipeline.sql' copies the file's current contents into the staging area. After adding, the file appears under 'Changes to be committed' and plain 'git diff' shows nothing for it, so you switch to 'git diff --staged' to see index-vs-HEAD - exactly what the commit will contain. 'git commit -m' writes that snapshot into a new commit with a message, and 'git log --oneline -1' shows it as the newest entry with its short SHA.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:

  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   pipeline.sql

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
diff --git a/pipeline.sql b/pipeline.sql

--- a/pipeline.sql
+++ b/pipeline.sql
@@ -12,7 +12,7 @@ FROM orders o
-JOIN customers c ON o.cust = c.id
+JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id

codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting that editing a file after 'git add' leaves the new edits unstaged - git status will list the file under BOTH staged and not-staged, and you must add again. Running 'git commit' with nothing staged commits nothing (or errors 'nothing to commit'). Using 'git commit -am' only stages already-tracked files, not brand-new (untracked) ones. Vague messages like 'fix' make history useless.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use 'git add -p pipeline.sql' to stage only some hunks and keep unrelated edits for a separate commit. Always run 'git diff --staged' right before committing to catch stray debug prints or credentials. Write the subject in the imperative ('Fix...', 'Add...') under ~50 characters, and add a body explaining WHY when the change is non-trivial.

codeExamples.title: Inspecting and searching history: log, show, blame, and per-file history
codeExamples.overview: Read the commit history compactly and graphically, inspect a single commit, attribute lines to commits, and follow the history of one pipeline file to find when a bug was introduced.
codeExamples.code:
# 1) Compact, one-line-per-commit view with branch topology
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -8

# 2) Which files each commit touched, and how much
git log --stat -3

# 3) Follow only the history of one file (the ETL model)
git log --oneline -- models/revenue.sql

# 4) Filter history: by author and by date window
git log --oneline --author="Priya" --since="2 weeks ago"

# 5) Inspect one commit in full: message + diff
git show a1b2c3d

# 6) See who last changed each line of the file, and in which commit
git blame models/revenue.sql

# 7) Search history for commits whose message mentions 'revenue'
git log --oneline --grep=revenue
codeExamples.breakdown: 'git log --oneline --graph --decorate' gives a compact, visual history with short SHAs and branch/tag labels; '-8' limits it to 8 commits. '--stat' adds a per-commit list of changed files. 'git log -- models/revenue.sql' restricts history to commits that touched that one file - the key move for tracing a file's evolution. '--author' and '--since' filter who and when; '--grep' searches commit messages. 'git show <sha>' prints a commit's metadata and full diff. 'git blame <file>' annotates each line with the commit, author, and date that last changed it, so you can jump from a suspect line straight to the commit that introduced it.

codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting the double dash in 'git log -- path' - without it Git may interpret the path as a revision. 'git blame' shows who last touched a line, not who introduced the bug, if the line was later reformatted; use 'git log -p -- file' to see the true origin. Long SHAs are unwieldy - abbreviate to the first 7-8 characters. On a huge repo, an unbounded 'git log' can flood the terminal; add -n or a path filter.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Alias a favorite log format (e.g. 'git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate"'). Combine filters: 'git log --oneline --since="2026-06-01" -- models/' scopes both time and path. Use 'git blame -L 10,20 file' to blame only a line range, and 'git log -S"customer_id" -- file' to find commits that added or removed that exact string (the 'pickaxe').

codeExamples.title: Undoing mistakes: unstage, discard, amend, revert - and the danger of reset --hard
codeExamples.overview: Safely back out of the common Git mistakes: unstage a file, discard local edits, fix the last commit, and undo a commit that is already pushed - contrasted with the destructive git reset --hard.
codeExamples.code:
# --- Unstage: keep the edits, just remove from the staging area ---
git restore --staged pipeline.sql   # (older syntax: git reset pipeline.sql)

# --- Discard working-directory edits entirely (DANGER: no undo) ---
git restore pipeline.sql            # reverts file to last committed state

# --- Fix the LAST commit: forgot a file or want a better message ---
git add models/revenue.sql
git commit --amend -m "Fix revenue join and add rollup model"
#   (only amend commits you have NOT pushed)

# --- Safely undo a commit that is ALREADY PUSHED: git revert ---
git revert a1b2c3d                  # creates a NEW commit that reverses a1b2c3d
#   history stays intact; safe to push and share

# --- Local-only reshaping: undo last commit but KEEP changes staged ---
git reset --soft HEAD~1             # commit undone, changes back in staging

# --- DESTRUCTIVE: throw away last commit AND all uncommitted work ---
git reset --hard HEAD~1             # permanent loss; never on shared branches
codeExamples.breakdown: 'git restore --staged file' removes a file from the index but leaves your edits on disk - the correct 'oops, wrong file staged' fix. 'git restore file' (no --staged) throws away your working-directory edits and cannot be undone. 'git commit --amend' replaces the previous commit with a new one (new SHA) so you can add a forgotten file or fix the message - only safe before pushing. 'git revert a1b2c3d' is the safe undo for a pushed commit: it adds a new inverse commit, preserving history. 'git reset --soft HEAD~1' undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged for recommit; 'git reset --hard HEAD~1' also erases the working directory - permanent data loss, never on shared history.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ git restore --staged pipeline.sql
$ git status
Changes not staged for commit:
	modified:   pipeline.sql

$ git commit --amend -m "Fix revenue join and add rollup model"
[main 9f8e7d6] Fix revenue join and add rollup model
 Date: Wed Jul 1 14:40:02 2026 +0000
 2 files changed, 6 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

$ git revert a1b2c3d
[main c0ffee1] Revert "Fix revenue join to use customer_id"
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)

$ git reset --soft HEAD~1
$ git status
Changes to be committed:
	modified:   pipeline.sql
codeExamples.commonIssues: Confusing 'git restore file' (discards edits, destructive) with 'git restore --staged file' (only unstages, safe). Amending a commit that is already pushed rewrites history and forces a painful force-push. Reaching for 'git reset --hard' to 'clean up' - it silently deletes uncommitted work with no recovery. Using reset instead of revert on a shared branch rewrites history everyone else has, causing conflicts for the whole team.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Default to 'git revert' for anything pushed; reserve 'git reset' for local, unshared commits. Before any 'reset --hard', run 'git stash' to park uncommitted work so it is recoverable. Use 'git reflog' as a safety net - it records where HEAD has been, so you can often recover a commit lost to a bad reset. Use '--soft' when you just want to redo the last commit's message or split it.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A finance dashboard's monthly revenue number suddenly looks wrong after a recent deploy. The data team must find which code change caused it, safely undo that change in a production repository without rewriting shared history, and redeploy - all while keeping the pipeline's Git history honest and auditable.
endToEndExample.inputData: A dbt project in a shared Git repository containing models/revenue.sql and related transformations, with several recent commits from multiple engineers, plus a .gitignore that keeps credentials (.env), local warehouse profiles, and large sample CSVs out of the repo.
endToEndExample.architecture: The workflow uses Git's three areas and history tools end to end: engineers edit models in the working directory, stage focused changes into the index, and commit atomic units; history is read with git log/show/blame to locate the offending commit; and the bad commit is neutralized with git revert (a new inverse commit) rather than git reset, so the shared, pushed history is never rewritten and production can be pinned to the resulting known-good SHA.
processingSteps: 1. Reproduce and scope: run 'git log --oneline -- models/revenue.sql' to list only the commits that touched the suspect model, and 'git log --since="3 days ago" --oneline' to focus on changes since the last known-good report.
2. Attribute the change: run 'git blame models/revenue.sql' to find which commit last modified the join line producing the wrong number, revealing SHA a1b2c3d and its author.
3. Confirm the cause: run 'git show a1b2c3d' to read the full diff and message, verifying that this commit changed the join in a way that double-counts revenue.

4. Undo safely: because a1b2c3d is already pushed and shared, run 'git revert a1b2c3d', which creates a new commit that inverts the bad join - preserving the full history including the mistake and its correction.
5. Review and verify: run 'git diff --staged' (or inspect the revert commit with 'git show') and 'git log --oneline -5' to confirm the revert is a clean, focused, atomic change before sharing it.
6. Ship and pin: push the revert commit, redeploy from the new known-good SHA, and record that SHA so production can be rolled back to it instantly if needed.
endToEndExample.output: A corrected revenue model, a new revert commit that transparently reverses the faulty change, and an intact, auditable history in which both the mistake and its fix are visible - plus a known-good commit SHA the team can pin production to.
endToEndExample.monitoring: git log --since / --author / '-- path' provides an audit trail of what changed and when; git blame attributes the suspect line to a specific commit and person; git show validates the exact diff being reverted, and git log --oneline confirms the revert landed as a single clean commit.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: The team deliberately uses git revert instead of git reset --hard so shared history is never rewritten and no engineer's local work is destroyed; had the bad commit been purely local and unpushed, git reset --soft would have been an option to reshape it before sharing.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A wrong dashboard number was traced to an exact commit with log/blame/show, reversed safely with git revert without rewriting shared history, and redeployed from a known-good SHA - demonstrating how staging discipline, atomic commits, and safe undo make production data pipelines auditable and quickly recoverable.

industryUseCases.problem: SQL and dbt model changes were deployed with little traceability, so when a metric broke it was hard to tell which change caused it or to roll back cleanly.
industryUseCases.solution: Adopt small atomic commits assembled via the staging area, review 'git diff --staged' before committing, and use git log/blame/show to trace metric bugs to a specific commit, reverting bad transformations with git revert.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fast root-cause analysis, safe one-command rollbacks, and an auditable history that ties every metric change to a reviewed, reversible commit.

industryUseCases.company: Data platform teams managing pipeline configuration and secrets
industryUseCases.problem: Engineers repeatedly risked committing credentials, local profiles, and large sample data files into shared repositories, bloating them and leaking secrets.
industryUseCases.solution: Standardize a .gitignore (for .env, __pycache__, *.csv, warehouse profiles) across repos, scan commits for secrets, and keep large data in object storage rather than Git.
industryUseCases.benefits: Lean, fast-cloning repositories, no leaked credentials, and a clear separation between versioned code and unversioned data and secrets.

industryUseCases.problem: A bad DAG or transformation deploy needed to be rolled back in production quickly and safely without rewriting the shared history other engineers depended on.
industryUseCases.solution: Pin production deploys to specific commit SHAs, and undo bad deploys with git revert (a new inverse commit) rather than git reset, redeploying from a known-good SHA.
industryUseCases.benefits: Instant, non-destructive rollbacks, reproducible deploys tied to exact commits, and a shared history that stays consistent for the whole team.

productionDeepDive.scalability: As repos and teams grow, atomic commits and clear messages keep code review and history navigation manageable, while a strict .gitignore and object storage (or Git LFS) for large data keep clone and CI times fast; monorepos add tooling to scope git log and diffs to changed paths.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Because commits are local until pushed, frequent pushes and protected branches guard against losing history to a dead laptop or a stray reset --hard; git reflog provides a local recovery net for commits accidentally dropped by a bad reset.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Hosted remotes (GitHub/GitLab) replicate the repository so the canonical history survives any single machine; CI/CD systems check out specific SHAs, so a healthy build can always be reproduced and redeployed independently of any individual's environment.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Pinning production to known-good commit SHAs makes rollback deterministic: revert or redeploy the prior SHA to restore service; keeping infrastructure and pipeline definitions in version control means a rebuilt environment can be restored to an exact past state.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Keep the repository small (no large binaries, sensible .gitignore) so clones and checkouts are fast in CI; use git log --oneline with path and date filters, and shallow clones in ephemeral CI runners, to keep operations responsive on long-lived histories.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Quick, correct git revert rollbacks shorten incidents and avoid wasted recompute and forensic labor; excluding data files from Git prevents storage and bandwidth costs multiplying across every engineer's clone and every CI run.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Keep secrets out with .gitignore, scan commits for credentials in CI, and enforce that a leaked secret is rotated immediately and purged from history (a later deletion commit is not enough); use signed commits and protected branches to prevent unauthorized or history-rewriting pushes.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Treat history as an audit log: use git log with --author/--since/'-- path' and git blame to answer 'what changed, when, by whom, and why' during incidents; require descriptive commit messages so the log itself is observable documentation.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Review 'git diff --staged' before every commit to ensure only intended changes ship (no debug output, no accidental data files, no secrets), and enforce code review on pull requests so transformation logic changes are validated before they can affect data.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Rely on descriptive, imperative commit messages with bodies explaining why as the primary change log; integrate CI to alert on failed builds, detected secrets, or attempts to force-push to protected branches so history rewrites and risky changes are caught early.

recommendedPractices: **Make atomic commits:** stage and commit one logical change at a time (use git add -p to split), so each commit is reviewable and independently revertible.
**Review before committing:** always run 'git diff --staged' to confirm the commit contains exactly what you intend - no debug prints, stray files, or secrets.
**Write good messages:** an imperative subject under ~50 chars ('Fix revenue join') plus a body explaining WHY the change was made.
**Undo pushed commits with revert, not reset:** use git revert for anything shared so history stays intact and reproducible.
**Maintain a .gitignore from day one:** exclude .env, credentials, __pycache__, and large data files so they never enter the repo.
engineeringStandards: Never commit secrets or large data files; keep them in .gitignore and store data in object storage or Git LFS.
Treat pushed history as immutable - reserve reset and --amend for local, unpushed commits only.
Require code review on changes to transformation and pipeline logic before they reach shared branches.
designRecommendations: Keep repositories focused and lean so history stays navigable and clones stay fast; split unrelated concerns into separate commits.
Structure work so each commit leaves the pipeline in a coherent, buildable state, enabling clean rollback to any SHA.
Prefer small, frequent commits over rare giant ones so bugs can be bisected and reverted precisely.
namingConventions: Write commit subjects in the imperative mood ('Add', 'Fix', 'Refactor'), not past tense, matching Git's own convention.
Reference the affected component or model in the subject (e.g. 'Fix revenue.sql join') so git log scans read clearly.
Use consistent .gitignore patterns across repos (*.csv, __pycache__/, .env) so exclusions are predictable.
documentationStandards: Use the commit body to document why a change was made, not just what, so future git blame/show gives real context.
Reference the ticket or incident in the commit message so history links back to the reason for the change.
Keep a README note on branch/commit conventions so the whole team produces consistent, readable history.
testingStrategies: Run the pipeline's tests or dbt build on the staged change before committing so each commit is known-good.
In CI, check out the exact commit SHA and validate it, so history and build artifacts stay reproducible.
Practice a revert on a scratch branch to confirm the rollback path works before you need it in an incident.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing everything with 'git add . && git commit -m "changes"' in one giant, unfocused blob.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is faster to type and skips the mental effort of deciding what belongs together; the value of atomic commits is not obvious until you need to review or revert one.
commonMistakes.impact: History becomes an unreadable list of vague mega-commits, code review is impossible, and you cannot revert one logical change without dragging along unrelated ones.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Stage deliberately - 'git add' the specific files or 'git add -p' the specific hunks for one logical change - review with 'git diff --staged', and commit it alone with a clear message before starting the next.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using 'git reset --hard' to undo a mistake, including on shared or pushed commits.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It feels like the definitive 'make it go away' command, and tutorials sometimes show it without warning that it destroys work and rewrites history.
commonMistakes.impact: Uncommitted work is permanently deleted with no undo, and on a shared branch the rewritten history conflicts with everyone else's, corrupting the team's repository.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: For pushed/shared commits use 'git revert' (a safe new inverse commit). For local reshaping use 'git reset --soft/--mixed', and stash first; keep 'reset --hard' for throwaway local state you are certain you do not need.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing credentials or large data files into the repository.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: A .env or sample CSV sits in the working directory, 'git add .' sweeps it up, and there is no .gitignore to exclude it.
commonMistakes.impact: Secrets leak into history (and remote clones) and remain even after later deletion, while large files bloat the repo and slow every clone and CI run.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Add a .gitignore before your first commit (excluding .env, credentials, *.csv, __pycache__), scan for secrets in CI, keep data in object storage, and if a secret slips in, rotate it and purge it from history immediately.

comparisonSection.explanation: git revert is additive and safe: it creates a new commit that applies the inverse of the target, so the bad change is neutralized while the full history stays intact - the correct choice for commits already pushed or shared. git reset --hard is subtractive and destructive: it moves the branch pointer back and permanently discards commits and uncommitted work, rewriting history - safe only on local, unshared commits. Rule of thumb: revert what is shared; reset only what is local.

comparisonSection.optionA: git diff (working directory vs staging area)
comparisonSection.optionB: git diff --staged (staging area vs last commit)
comparisonSection.explanation: Plain 'git diff' shows changes you have made but not yet staged - what 'git add' would pick up next. 'git diff --staged' (aka --cached) shows what is already staged - exactly what your next commit will contain. After you 'git add' a file it moves from the first view to the second. Use plain diff to review edits before staging, and --staged right before committing to confirm the commit's contents are precisely what you intend.

git add copies a file's current contents into the staging area as a proposal for the next snapshot - it does not save anything into history, and edits made after adding are not staged. git commit takes the staged snapshot and records it permanently as an immutable commit with a message, parent, and SHA. Neither, however, backs work up remotely - that requires git push. The pipeline is: edit (working dir) -> git add (staged) -> git commit (local history) -> git push (shared/backed up).

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the three areas Git uses, and what does each represent?
beginnerQuestions.answer: The working directory holds the actual files you edit on disk. The staging area (or index) holds the changes you have marked with 'git add' to include in the next commit. The repository (the .git directory) holds the committed history - the permanent snapshots. The everyday flow is: edit in the working directory, stage selected changes into the index, then commit them into the repository.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The interviewer wants the core mental model. Emphasizing that staging is a deliberate middle step - not automatic - shows you understand why Git works the way it does.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between git add and git commit?
beginnerQuestions.answer: git add copies the current contents of files into the staging area as a proposal for the next commit - it does not record anything in history, and if you edit the file again those new edits are not staged. git commit takes whatever is staged and records it permanently as an immutable commit with a message, a parent, and a unique SHA. Add queues; commit records.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This tests the very common 'git add saves my work' misconception. Bonus points for noting that neither backs the work up remotely - that is git push.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you find out which commit introduced a bug in a specific pipeline file?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Start with 'git log --oneline -- path/to/pipeline.sql' to see only the commits that touched that file, optionally narrowing with --since or --author. Use 'git blame path/to/pipeline.sql' to see which commit last changed the suspect line, then 'git show <sha>' to read that commit's full diff and message. If blame points to a later reformat rather than the true origin, use 'git log -p -- file' or the pickaxe 'git log -S"<string>" -- file' to find where the logic actually changed.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This checks practical forensic skill. Naming log path-filtering, blame, and show - plus the caveat that blame shows the last change, not necessarily the introducing one - signals real experience.

intermediateQuestions.question: When would you use git revert versus git reset, and why?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Use git revert to undo a commit that has already been pushed or shared: it adds a new commit that inverts the change, so history stays intact and everyone's repository remains consistent. Use git reset only on local, unpushed commits to reshape them - '--soft' keeps changes staged, '--mixed' unstages them, '--hard' discards them entirely. Reset rewrites history, so on a shared branch it corrupts everyone else's copy; revert is the safe, shareable undo.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The key insight is safe (revert, preserves history) versus destructive (reset, rewrites history) and the shared-vs-local rule. Explaining the three reset modes shows depth.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the three git reset modes and exactly what each one touches.
advancedQuestions.answer: git reset moves the current branch pointer to a target commit and differs by how much else it changes. '--soft <ref>' moves only the pointer, leaving the index and working directory untouched, so the undone commit's changes remain staged - ideal for redoing the last commit's message or splitting it. '--mixed <ref>' (the default) also resets the index to match the target, so the changes become unstaged edits in the working directory. '--hard <ref>' additionally overwrites the working directory to match the target, permanently discarding those changes. Soft and mixed are recoverable (your work stays on disk); hard destroys uncommitted work with no undo except via reflog.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This tests precise understanding of Git's internals: the branch pointer, index, and working tree, and which mode moves which. Mentioning reflog as a recovery net is a strong signal.

advancedQuestions.question: A secret was accidentally committed and pushed. Why is deleting it in a new commit insufficient, and what should you do?
advancedQuestions.answer: A commit is an immutable snapshot; deleting the secret in a later commit leaves it fully present in the earlier commit, which anyone with clone access can still read. The correct response is: first rotate/revoke the secret immediately (assume it is compromised), then rewrite history to purge it from all commits using a tool like git filter-repo or BFG, and force-update the remote, coordinating with the team since history changes. Prevent recurrence with a .gitignore entry and CI secret scanning.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This probes understanding that history is immutable and append-only by default. The critical, non-obvious point is rotate first - purging history does not un-leak an already-exposed secret.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You have edited five files while fixing a bug and also did some unrelated refactoring in one of them. You want the bug fix to be one clean, reviewable commit and the refactor to be a separate commit. How do you do it with Git's staging area?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The goal is two atomic commits from a mixed set of changes, which is exactly what the staging area is for. First inspect what changed with git status and git diff. For the files that belong entirely to the bug fix, git add them directly. For the one file that mixes bug fix and refactor, use interactive/partial staging (git add -p) to stage only the bug-fix hunks. Then verify with git diff --staged that only the bug fix is queued, commit it, and finally add and commit the remaining refactor changes as the second commit.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Run 'git status' and 'git diff' to see all changes. 'git add' the files that are purely part of the bug fix. For the file mixing concerns, run 'git add -p <file>' and answer y/n per hunk to stage only the bug-fix hunks. Confirm with 'git diff --staged' that only the fix is queued, then 'git commit -m "Fix ..."'. Now the refactor hunks remain unstaged; 'git add' them and 'git commit -m "Refactor ..."' as a second, separate commit. The result is two focused, independently revertible commits from one working session.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design how a data engineering team should version and operate their SQL/dbt/pipeline code in Git so changes are reviewable, secrets and data stay out of the repo, and production can be rolled back safely.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Enforce small atomic commits assembled via the staging area with descriptive imperative messages, reviewed on pull requests before merge. Maintain a strict .gitignore (.env, credentials, *.csv, __pycache__) and keep large data in object storage or Git LFS. Pin production deploys to specific commit SHAs in CI/CD, undo bad deploys with git revert (never reset on shared history), and use git log/blame/show plus CI secret scanning for auditing and safety.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Requiring review and atomic commits adds process overhead but yields readable, revertible history and safer deploys. Using revert instead of reset keeps history honest and shareable at the cost of extra 'revert' commits. Keeping data out of Git means a separate storage system but avoids repo bloat and leaks. Protected branches and signed commits add friction but prevent destructive history rewrites.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: As the team grows, adopt branch protection, required reviews, and CI checks (tests, secret scanning) on every change; scope git operations by path in large/monorepos, use shallow clones in ephemeral CI, and rely on pinned SHAs plus git revert so rollbacks stay deterministic and reproducible across many engineers and environments.

followUpQuestions: What is the difference between HEAD, HEAD~1, and a commit SHA, and when do you use each?
How does 'git commit --amend' change the commit, and why is it dangerous after pushing?
What does git stash do, and how does it help before a risky reset?
How is 'git restore file' different from 'git restore --staged file'?
What is git reflog and how can it recover a commit lost to 'git reset --hard'?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Git tracks work across three areas - the working directory (edits), the staging area/index (git add: queued for the next commit), and the repository (git commit: permanent hashed history) - while log/show/blame read history, .gitignore keeps files out, and revert (safe) or reset (destructive) undo changes.
keyConcepts: Three areas: working directory (edits) -> staging area/index (git add) -> repository (git commit); push is separate and backs up remotely.
git add stages a snapshot for the next commit; it does not save work, and edits made after adding are not staged.
git diff shows unstaged (working vs index) changes; git diff --staged shows what the next commit will contain (index vs HEAD).
Reference commits by SHA, HEAD, HEAD~1, HEAD~3; each commit is an immutable snapshot pointing to its parent.
git revert adds a safe inverse commit (use for pushed history); git reset --soft/--mixed/--hard rewrites history (local only; --hard destroys work).
commands: git status                       # see untracked, modified, and staged files
git add -p pipeline.sql          # stage selected hunks; git diff --staged to review
git commit -m "Fix revenue join" # record staged snapshot with an imperative message
git log --oneline --graph -- models/revenue.sql  # history of one file
git blame models/revenue.sql     # who/which commit last changed each line; git show <sha>
git revert a1b2c3d               # safe undo of a pushed commit (new inverse commit)
interviewPoints: Three areas: working dir, staging/index, repository; add queues, commit records, push backs up.
git add != save; only commit records history, and post-add edits are unstaged.
revert = safe inverse commit (pushed history); reset --hard = destructive rewrite (local only).
reset modes: --soft keeps staged, --mixed unstages, --hard discards working-dir changes.
Use log/blame/show to trace a bug to a commit; .gitignore keeps secrets and data out.
quickNotes: 'git restore file' discards edits (destructive); 'git restore --staged file' only unstages (safe).
'git commit -am' stages tracked modifications only - not brand-new untracked files.
A commit is local until 'git push' - committed does not mean backed up remotely.
'git commit --amend' rewrites the last commit; never amend after pushing shared history.
'git reflog' can recover commits lost to a bad reset; add .gitignore before the first commit.

keyTakeaways: Git works across three areas: the working directory (files you edit), the staging area/index (what git add queues for the next commit), and the repository (the permanent, hashed history that git commit writes) - and git status and git diff let you see exactly what is modified, staged, and committed.

The staging area exists so you can craft focused, atomic commits: use git add (and git add -p for partial staging) to include only one logical change, review it with git diff --staged, and commit it alone with a clear imperative message and a body explaining why.

Read and search history with git log (--oneline/--graph/--stat/--author/--since/'-- path'), git show <sha>, and git blame, referencing commits by SHA, HEAD, and HEAD~n - the everyday tools for tracing when and why a pipeline bug was introduced.

Undo safely versus destructively: git revert adds a new inverse commit and is the right choice for anything already pushed, while git reset --soft/--mixed/--hard rewrites history and should stay on local, unpushed commits - and --hard permanently discards uncommitted work.

Operationally, keep secrets and large data files out with .gitignore, remember that committing is local (only git push backs work up remotely and shares it), and pin production to known-good SHAs so a bad transformation can be reverted and redeployed quickly and auditably.
